opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was one of the things that surprised me a bit when we were putting the training mix together. The conventional wisdom is that you pretrain on a big pile of web text, code, books, and then afterwards you do instruction tuning and maybe some preference optimization to turn the base model into something that can actually hold a conversation. That's a very clean separation, but it's also somewhat arbitrary. There's nothing fundamental that says the model has to learn "how to be a language model" first and "how to follow instructions" only at the very end.

So what we did was mix a decent amount of instruction data, already formatted with the chat template, directly into pretraining. Part of the motivation was practical. As an academic group we didn't have the budget for an elaborate post-training pipeline, so we wanted a model that would come out of pretraining already reasonably usable. But it also turned out to be interesting from a research perspective.

One thing you notice is that the model internalizes the template very early. The special tokens, the turn structure, the idea that there's a user and an assistant and that a response ends at a certain point. All of that gets picked up as just another regularity in the data. When you only see it in a short fine-tuning phase at the end, it can feel more brittle, a bit like a format the model has been coaxed into. When it's present the whole time, it becomes part of the model's basic understanding of what text looks like.

The other interesting aspect is that it blurs the line between a base model and a chat model. Evaluations get more interesting too, because you can run conversational or instruction-following evals on intermediate checkpoints and watch that capability develop alongside everything else, rather than having it appear suddenly after post-training. That gives you a much better picture of when reasoning or instruction-following behaviors emerge during training.

Of course there are trade-offs. You need to be careful about the proportion. Too much instruction data and you risk the model overfitting to a narrow style, or you contaminate your benchmarks if you're not careful with what's in that data. And it makes the base model less "neutral," if you want a purely unconditioned language model for research. But overall I think it's an underexplored design choice, and the fact that it worked reasonably well for us suggests that the strict pretraining versus post-training split is more of a convention than a necessity.

r001.rationale: The response says the academic group lacked the budget for an elaborate post-training pipeline and wanted a model that was usable after pretraining, giving the practical motivation for mixing in instruction data and chat templates.

r002.rationale: It says conversational and instruction-following evaluations can be run on intermediate checkpoints, communicating that those checkpoints can be used conversationally during training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that I think a lot of people find a little surprising, because the conventional recipe is very staged. You pretrain on a big pile of web text, then you do a separate instruction tuning phase, maybe some preference optimization after that, and there's a kind of folk wisdom that you shouldn't contaminate the pretraining stage with any of that. We just didn't do that. We mixed instruction data into pretraining and we trained with the chat template from the very beginning.

The thing I find interesting is what it tells you about where the model's behavior actually comes from. If you look at what instruction tuning does in the standard pipeline, a lot of it is really just teaching the model the format. It's learning that there's a user turn and an assistant turn, that there's a certain register it should respond in, that it should stop at the right place. That's a pretty shallow thing to be learning in a dedicated phase at the end, and in our case we didn't have to spend a separate phase on it at all. The model just knew the format because it had seen it millions of times during training. When you talk to it right out of pretraining, it already behaves like a chat model.

The second piece, and this is the one I care more about for our setup, is that we're interested in reasoning, in the model doing more computation per token through recurrence, and it turns out that having the data look like problems and solutions during pretraining matters for that. Raw web text has a lot of content, but it rarely has the structure of "here is a question, here is a worked answer." Instruction data has exactly that structure. So mixing it in gives the model a lot of exposure to the kind of thing we actually want it to be good at, instead of hoping that capability emerges and then getting surfaced later by fine-tuning.

And then there's a more pragmatic point, which is that with a small team and a limited compute budget, you don't want to maintain three or four separate training stages where each one has its own hyperparameters and its own data mix and its own failure modes. Collapsing it into one run makes the whole thing simpler to reason about. You can look at the model at any checkpoint during training and just ask it things, and that's really useful for understanding what it's learning as it goes.

I'd also say, honestly, I don't think the staged approach is sacred. It came about historically because the instruction data didn't exist when people started pretraining, and it got layered on afterward. Now there's plenty of it, and I think the interesting question is why you wouldn't put it in early. The answer we got is that there's no particular reason not to, and a few pretty good reasons to do it.

r001.rationale: The response says limited compute motivated avoiding several separate training stages by mixing instruction data into pretraining, eliminating the need for a separate post-training phase.

r002.rationale: It says the model can be queried at any checkpoint during training, and that training with chat templates from the beginning makes it behave like a chat model.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that the boundary between pretraining and instruction tuning is somewhat artificial. During pretraining, we’re already teaching the model to continue text in all kinds of formats. A conversation with user and assistant turns is another format, so why shouldn’t it encounter that early on?

Including instruction data with a chat template gives the model a chance to learn both the content and how that content is used in an interaction. It can learn that a user asks a question and the assistant responds, rather than having to pick up that structure entirely in a separate stage afterward.

The interesting question is how much that buys you. Does it make subsequent instruction tuning easier? Does the model become better at using what it learned during pretraining to answer questions? And how much instruction data do you need in the mixture? I wouldn’t assume this replaces post-training, but it’s a useful way to question which parts of the pipeline really need to be separate.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that the boundary between pretraining and instruction tuning is a little artificial. During pretraining, we teach a model to continue text, and then afterward we teach it that some of that text is a user asking a question and some is an assistant answering it. But you can introduce that structure much earlier.

A chat template gives the model explicit information about who is speaking and where an instruction ends and a response begins. And instruction data gives it examples of what it means to actually carry out a task, rather than just continue a document. So the question is: does learning those things throughout training make the model better at using its capabilities when you ask it to do something?

There’s a tradeoff, of course. You still want the breadth of ordinary pretraining data, and you don’t want the model to become overly specialized to a particular format. But I think it’s an interesting way to ask how much of instruction following really needs to be a separate, final stage of training.
